pa-pharm-l01.q: Digoxin distributes heavily into muscle and other tissue, giving it a very large volume of distribution, while a drug that stays mostly in the bloodstream has a small one. What does a large volume of distribution predict about dosing?
choices: The drug needs a loading dose because waiting 4-5 half-lives to fill that large space would delay effect too long
The drug needs a smaller total dose because it is diluted so widely
The drug cannot be given IV
The drug will have 100% bioavailability regardless of route
pa-pharm-l01.why: A large volume of distribution means most of the drug leaves the bloodstream for tissue, so a loading dose is used to fill that space immediately rather than waiting through several half-lives. It does not shrink the needed dose (the opposite: more total drug is needed to reach a given blood level), route of administration is a separate question, and volume of distribution has nothing to do with bioavailability.

pa-pharm-l01.q: A hypotensive trauma patient needs an emergency drug and peripheral IV access cannot be obtained. Why is intraosseous (IO) access chosen over an intramuscular injection?
choices: IO delivers the drug straight into a marrow space that drains to the central circulation almost as fast as IV, while IM depends on muscle perfusion that shock has already shut down
IO injections are less painful than IM injections
IM absorption is faster than IO in every patient
IO access requires no special equipment
pa-pharm-l01.why: Bone marrow behaves like a non-collapsible vein, so an IO drug reaches the circulation in seconds, matching IV onset even in shock. IM absorption depends on blood flow to muscle, which is exactly what shock diverts away. Comfort is irrelevant in an emergency, and IO placement does require a dedicated drill or needle device.

pa-pharm-l02.q: An 82-year-old with mild dementia is given diphenhydramine 50 mg for itching and becomes acutely more confused. What principle from this lesson explains why this drug is a poor choice in older adults?
choices: Older adults have lower glomerular filtration, less albumin, and more body fat, so the Beers criteria list diphenhydramine as a drug to avoid after 65
Diphenhydramine is a prodrug that only activates in young patients
Older adults metabolize diphenhydramine faster, so the dose was too low
Confusion after diphenhydramine only occurs with IV administration
pa-pharm-l02.why: Reduced kidney and liver clearance plus altered body composition make older adults especially sensitive to sedating anticholinergics, and diphenhydramine is on the Beers list of drugs to avoid for this reason. It is not a prodrug, older adults clear many drugs more slowly rather than faster, and the confusion risk applies to oral dosing too.

pa-pharm-l02.q: A pregnant patient with a urinary tract infection is prescribed a fluoroquinolone by a covering provider. What is the concern from this lesson's pregnancy list?
choices: Fluoroquinolones are on the short list of drugs with an absolute avoid-in-pregnancy recommendation, along with ACE inhibitors, warfarin, isotretinoin, and tetracyclines
Fluoroquinolones are safe in pregnancy but dangerous while breastfeeding only
The only pregnancy concern with antibiotics is allergy
Fluoroquinolones are avoided only in the third trimester
pa-pharm-l02.why: Fluoroquinolones sit on the absolute avoid list for pregnancy in this lesson, alongside ACE inhibitors/ARBs, warfarin, isotretinoin, and tetracyclines, because of documented fetal harm rather than theoretical risk. The concern applies throughout pregnancy, not just the third trimester, and it is a fetal safety issue, not simply an allergy question.

pa-pharm-l03.q: A patient maintained on buprenorphine for opioid use disorder is given a full dose of morphine for acute pain and develops sudden withdrawal symptoms. What explains this?
choices: Buprenorphine's high affinity for the mu receptor let it displace the morphine, and as a partial agonist it produces less effect than the full agonist it replaced, precipitating withdrawal
Morphine destroyed the buprenorphine in the bloodstream
Buprenorphine is a pure antagonist like naloxone
The patient became allergic to morphine
pa-pharm-l03.why: Buprenorphine grips the mu receptor tightly enough to outcompete a full agonist, but because it is only a partial agonist it delivers less total effect, so a patient can be thrown into withdrawal. It is not a pure antagonist (that is naloxone), there is no chemical destruction of morphine in blood, and this is a pharmacologic effect, not an allergy.

pa-pharm-l03.q: Lithium, phenytoin, and vancomycin all get blood levels drawn routinely. What single property do they share that makes this necessary?
choices: A narrow therapeutic index, meaning the toxic dose is close to the effective dose so small changes in level matter
They are all antibiotics
They all have a wide therapeutic index and monitoring is just a formality
They are all given only by the oral route
pa-pharm-l03.why: A narrow therapeutic index means the gap between an effective level and a toxic level is small, so routine levels catch trouble before it becomes dangerous. Lithium is a mood stabilizer and vancomycin is an antibiotic, not all three are antibiotics, and a wide therapeutic index would make monitoring unnecessary, not required. Route varies among these three drugs.

pa-pharm-l04.q: An order calls for lidocaine 2% for a nerve block. How many milligrams are in each milliliter of a 2% solution?
choices: 20 mg/mL
2 mg/mL
200 mg/mL
0.2 mg/mL
pa-pharm-l04.why: A 1% solution is 10 mg/mL (1 g per 100 mL), so a 2% solution is 20 mg/mL. Reading the percent as the milligram count directly (2 mg/mL) ignores the definition, and the other two options are off by a factor of ten in either direction.

pa-pharm-l04.q: Why are dangerous abbreviations like a trailing zero (writing 1.0 mg instead of 1 mg) banned in most hospitals?
choices: 1.0 mg can be misread as 10 mg if the decimal point is missed, causing a tenfold overdose
Trailing zeros make the order take longer to write
Trailing zeros are only a problem with oral medications
The ban only applies to pediatric orders
pa-pharm-l04.why: A decimal point that is missed or smudged turns 1.0 mg into what reads as 10 mg, a tenfold error, which is why the standard is always to write a leading zero (0.5 mg) and never a trailing one. This risk applies to any route, and it is a general medication-safety rule, not one limited to children.

pa-pharm-l05.q: A patient with known aspirin-sensitive asthma is given ibuprofen for a headache and develops sudden wheezing. What is the mechanism?
choices: NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase, shifting arachidonic acid metabolism toward leukotrienes, which can trigger bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma
Ibuprofen is a beta blocker and worsens bronchospasm
This is a classic IgE-mediated allergic reaction to ibuprofen
NSAIDs directly paralyze the diaphragm
pa-pharm-l05.why: Blocking cyclooxygenase diverts arachidonic acid down the lipoxygenase pathway, producing more bronchoconstricting leukotrienes, which is why NSAIDs can trigger severe bronchospasm in a subset of asthmatics. This is a pharmacologic pseudo-allergic reaction, not IgE-mediated, ibuprofen has no beta-blocking activity, and the diaphragm is not affected.

pa-pharm-l05.q: Bupivacaine is favored for a longer-lasting nerve block but carries the greatest risk if injected into a blood vessel. What is that specific risk?
choices: It is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic, and systemic toxicity progresses from perioral tingling and metallic taste to seizures and arrhythmia
It causes permanent nerve damage at any dose
It cannot be reversed if toxicity occurs
It has no effect on the heart, only the central nervous system
pa-pharm-l05.why: Bupivacaine binds cardiac sodium channels more avidly than other local anesthetics, so accidental intravascular injection can rapidly progress from early warning signs (tingling lips, metallic taste, tinnitus) to seizures and lethal arrhythmia. Lipid emulsion is the specific rescue therapy, so toxicity is not untreatable, and long block duration at normal doses does not cause permanent nerve injury.

pa-pharm-l06.q: A chronic benzodiazepine user who also took a tricyclic antidepressant is given flumazenil to reverse sedation. Why is this considered dangerous?
choices: Flumazenil can strip away GABA inhibition the patient depends on, provoking seizures that cannot then be controlled with a benzodiazepine
Flumazenil raises blood pressure to dangerous levels
Flumazenil has no effect in chronic benzodiazepine users
Flumazenil causes immediate cardiac arrest in everyone
pa-pharm-l06.why: Chronic benzodiazepine use or a co-ingested tricyclic both lower the seizure threshold once GABA-A inhibition is abruptly removed, and because benzodiazepines are the usual seizure treatment, this can leave a seizure that is very hard to stop. It does not reliably raise blood pressure or cause immediate arrest, and it very much does have an effect in chronic users, that effect is the danger.

pa-pharm-l06.q: Dexmedetomidine is chosen for sedating an intubated or alcohol-withdrawing patient instead of a benzodiazepine drip. What makes it useful in this setting?
choices: As an alpha-2 agonist it sedates without significantly depressing respiratory drive, at the cost of bradycardia and hypotension
It has no side effects at any dose
It works through the same GABA-A mechanism as benzodiazepines but is stronger
It reverses respiratory depression from opioids
pa-pharm-l06.why: Dexmedetomidine sedates through alpha-2 receptors rather than GABA-A, so it largely spares the respiratory drive that benzodiazepines and opioids blunt, which is valuable in an intubated or withdrawing patient, though bradycardia and hypotension are real trade-offs. It shares no mechanism with GABA-A drugs and does not reverse opioid effects the way naloxone does.

pa-pharm-l07.q: A patient on gentamicin for a serious gram-negative infection needs monitoring beyond peak and trough drug levels. What two organ systems are specifically at risk?
choices: Kidney and inner ear (hearing/balance)
Liver and pancreas
Thyroid and adrenal gland
Bone marrow and skin
pa-pharm-l07.why: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin concentrate in the kidney and inner ear, causing nephrotoxicity and permanent, dose-related hearing or vestibular loss, which is why levels and renal function are tracked closely. Liver, pancreas, thyroid, adrenal, marrow, and skin are not the characteristic aminoglycoside targets.

pa-pharm-l07.q: An older patient on chronic prednisone is started on levofloxacin and days later reports sudden heel pain after a minor jump. What is the concern?
choices: Fluoroquinolone-associated tendon rupture, a risk that is higher in older adults and in patients on corticosteroids
This is an unrelated overuse injury with no drug connection
Levofloxacin caused an allergic reaction in the tendon
The prednisone alone, without the fluoroquinolone, explains the rupture
pa-pharm-l07.why: Fluoroquinolones weaken collagen and can cause tendinopathy or frank rupture, most often the Achilles tendon, and the risk climbs with age and concurrent corticosteroid use, exactly this patient's situation. It is a recognized drug effect rather than a coincidence, and it is not an IgE-mediated allergic process.

pa-pharm-l08.q: A patient with a creatinine clearance of 22 mL/min is started on enoxaparin for a deep vein thrombosis. What adjustment is required?
choices: The dose must be reduced because enoxaparin is renally cleared and accumulates in significant kidney impairment
No adjustment is needed because enoxaparin is hepatically cleared
The dose should be doubled to overcome poor absorption
Enoxaparin should be switched to aspirin automatically
pa-pharm-l08.why: Low molecular weight heparin is cleared by the kidney, so a creatinine clearance under about 30 mL/min requires a reduced dose to avoid drug accumulation and bleeding. It is not hepatically cleared, doubling the dose would compound the risk, and switching to an antiplatelet does not treat venous thrombosis the same way.

pa-pharm-l08.q: Aspirin is given once in suspected heart attack but its antiplatelet effect lasts far longer than one dose would suggest. Why?
choices: Aspirin irreversibly disables cyclooxygenase in each platelet for that platelet's entire 7-10 day lifespan, since platelets cannot make new enzyme
Aspirin is stored in fat and slowly released over days
Aspirin's active metabolite has an extremely long half-life
The effect actually wears off within 2 hours
pa-pharm-l08.why: Platelets have no nucleus and cannot synthesize new cyclooxygenase, so a single irreversible hit from aspirin disables that platelet for the rest of its 7-10 day life, and new platelets restore function gradually as they are made. This is not a storage or metabolite half-life effect, and the action is far longer-lasting than 2 hours.

pa-pharm-l09.q: A patient needs a beta blocker for rate control but the team wants the option to stop the effect quickly if it is not tolerated. Which drug fits and why?
choices: Esmolol, because its effect lasts only about 9 minutes
Metoprolol, because it can be given IV
Labetalol, because it blocks both alpha and beta receptors
Propranolol, because it is non-selective
pa-pharm-l09.why: Esmolol's ultra-short duration of roughly 9 minutes makes it the choice when the team wants to test a beta blocker's effect with an easy ability to let it wear off. Metoprolol being IV does not shorten its duration, labetalol's dual blockade does not make it short-acting, and non-selectivity is unrelated to duration.

pa-pharm-l09.q: Diltiazem is generally avoided in a patient with a weak, reduced-ejection-fraction heart. What is the concern?
choices: Its negative inotropic effect can further depress an already weak heart's pumping function
It has no effect on cardiac contractility
It only affects blood vessels, never the heart itself
It is contraindicated only because of kidney clearance
pa-pharm-l09.why: Diltiazem and verapamil act on the heart itself, and their negative inotropic effect can push a failing heart further into decompensation, which is why they are avoided in reduced ejection fraction heart failure. They are not vessel-only drugs like amlodipine, and the caution is about contractility, not kidney clearance.

pa-pharm-l10.q: A patient with contrast-enhanced CT scheduled needs metformin addressed. What is the reasoning?
choices: Metformin can accumulate if acute kidney injury follows contrast exposure, raising the risk of lactic acidosis
Metformin interferes directly with the contrast dye's imaging quality
Metformin must always be stopped permanently before any imaging
There is no real interaction and metformin can be continued without thought
pa-pharm-l10.why: Metformin is held around contrast administration because contrast-associated kidney injury can let the drug accumulate and precipitate lactic acidosis, a rare but serious complication. It does not affect image quality, the hold is typically temporary rather than permanent, and ignoring the interaction is not the safe approach.

pa-pharm-l10.q: A patient on a sulfonylurea overdoses and is treated with repeated dextrose boluses in the emergency department. Why can the hypoglycemia keep recurring for hours?
choices: Sulfonylureas stimulate ongoing insulin release, so each dextrose bolus provokes more insulin secretion and another drop in glucose, requiring admission for observation
Dextrose does not work on sulfonylurea overdose
The hypoglycemia is unrelated to the drug and is caused by fasting
Sulfonylureas are cleared within 30 minutes so this should not happen
pa-pharm-l10.why: Sulfonylureas keep triggering pancreatic insulin release, so glucose given to treat one low can provoke the next low as insulin secretion continues, which is why these patients are admitted for monitoring rather than treated and discharged. Dextrose does raise glucose temporarily, the hypoglycemia is drug-driven, not fasting-related, and sulfonylurea effects can last many hours.

pa-pharm-l11.q: A patient with a deep, spreading skin infection has pain far out of proportion to the exam, skin anesthesia over part of the area, and crepitus. What does this combination suggest and what is the treatment?
choices: Necrotizing fasciitis, requiring emergency surgical debridement plus vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and clindamycin
Simple cellulitis, treated with oral cephalexin
An abscess needing bedside incision and drainage only
A drug allergy requiring only antihistamines
pa-pharm-l11.why: Pain out of proportion, anesthesia from nerve destruction, and crepitus from gas-forming organisms are red flags for necrotizing fasciitis, a surgical emergency where antibiotics (including clindamycin for its toxin-suppressing effect) support but do not replace debridement. This picture goes well beyond simple cellulitis or an abscess, and it is not an allergic reaction.

pa-pharm-l11.q: A patient is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease. What treatment approach is correct?
choices: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days, covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes together
Doxycycline alone for 7 days
A single dose of azithromycin only
No antibiotics until cultures return
pa-pharm-l11.why: PID is typically polymicrobial, so treatment covers gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes together with ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole for 14 days rather than treating one organism alone. Waiting for cultures delays treatment of a condition that risks tubal scarring and infertility, and single-agent or single-dose regimens leave gaps in coverage.

pa-pharm-l12.q: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is already on an ACE inhibitor, carvedilol, and spironolactone. Which addition has been shown to lower mortality regardless of whether the patient has diabetes?
choices: An SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin
Furosemide
Digoxin
Amlodipine
pa-pharm-l12.why: SGLT2 inhibitors are the fourth mortality-lowering pillar in HFrEF and help whether or not the patient has diabetes. Furosemide relieves congestion but has not been shown to extend life, digoxin reduces hospitalization but not mortality, and amlodipine is not one of the four pillar therapies.

pa-pharm-l12.q: A patient in new atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate is hemodynamically stable. The team debates rate control versus attempting rhythm control. What does the evidence support?
choices: Overall survival was similar between strategies in older trials, but rhythm control started within the first year of diagnosis improves outcomes
Rhythm control is always harmful and should never be attempted
Rate control has been proven superior in every situation
The choice has no bearing on outcomes at any time point
pa-pharm-l12.why: Classic trials found similar survival between rate and rhythm control strategies overall, but more recent evidence shows that starting rhythm control early, within the first year, improves outcomes. Rhythm control is not universally harmful, rate control has not been shown categorically superior, and timing does matter.

pa-pharm-l13.q: Why is scheduled acetaminophen and NSAID dosing preferred over as-needed dosing for postoperative pain?
choices: Chasing pain that has already peaked requires more drug than staying ahead of it with scheduled, multimodal dosing
As-needed dosing is always cheaper for the patient
Scheduled dosing avoids the need for any opioid ever
As-needed dosing causes more side effects than scheduled dosing
pa-pharm-l13.why: Multimodal, scheduled non-opioid dosing keeps pain from peaking in the first place, so less total drug (including less opioid) is needed compared with waiting until pain is severe and then trying to catch up. Cost is not the reason given, scheduled dosing reduces but does not eliminate opioid need in significant pain, and side effects depend on the drug and dose, not the schedule alone.

pa-pharm-l13.q: A chronic opioid user develops respiratory depression from an overdose. Why is naloxone given in small 0.04 mg increments rather than the full 0.4-2 mg dose used in a naive patient?
choices: A tolerant patient can be reversed enough to breathe without stripping every receptor and triggering severe, violent withdrawal
Small doses work faster than large doses
The tolerant patient requires no naloxone at all
Small doses avoid any risk of re-sedation
pa-pharm-l13.why: Titrating naloxone in small steps restores adequate breathing while minimizing the abrupt, complete receptor blockade that would precipitate severe withdrawal in a physically dependent patient. Small doses are not inherently faster, tolerant overdose patients still need naloxone, and re-sedation risk remains once naloxone wears off regardless of the titration strategy.

pa-pharm-l14.q: A patient stops venlafaxine abruptly after months of use and develops dizziness, electric shock sensations, and irritability within a day. What is happening and what class of drug is most associated with this?
choices: Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome, most notably with paroxetine and venlafaxine due to their short half-lives
A new psychiatric illness unrelated to the medication
Serotonin syndrome from too much venlafaxine
This only happens with tricyclic antidepressants
pa-pharm-l14.why: Paroxetine and venlafaxine have relatively short half-lives, so stopping them abruptly produces a flu-like discontinuation syndrome with sensory disturbances, which is why they should be tapered. This is not serotonin syndrome (which comes from excess serotonergic activity, not withdrawal), it is a recognized pharmacologic phenomenon rather than a new illness, and it is not exclusive to tricyclics.

pa-pharm-l14.q: A patient has been on an antipsychotic for over a year and develops slow, involuntary chewing and tongue-thrusting movements. How does this differ from acute dystonia in timing and reversibility?
choices: This is tardive dyskinesia, which appears after months to years and is often permanent, unlike dystonia which appears in hours to days and resolves with treatment
It is acute dystonia and will resolve within minutes of diphenhydramine
It is akathisia, treated the same way as dystonia
Involuntary orofacial movements always indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome
pa-pharm-l14.why: Tardive dyskinesia develops after prolonged exposure (months to years) and is frequently irreversible even after stopping the drug, in sharp contrast to acute dystonia, which appears within hours to days and responds promptly to anticholinergics. Akathisia is inner restlessness, not orofacial movements, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents with rigidity and fever, not isolated dyskinesia.

pa-pharm-l15.q: Using the formula age in years divided by 4 plus 4, what uncuffed endotracheal tube size is appropriate for an 8-year-old?
pa-pharm-l15.why: Eight divided by 4 is 2, plus 4 gives a tube size of 6.0 for an uncuffed tube. The other values come from skipping the division step, using the age directly, or a miscalculation of the addition.

pa-pharm-l15.q: A 15 kg child is in pulseless ventricular fibrillation. What is the correct first defibrillation energy?
choices: 30 J (2 J/kg)
15 J (1 J/kg)
60 J (4 J/kg)
150 J, the adult biphasic dose
pa-pharm-l15.why: The first pediatric defibrillation dose is 2 J/kg, so 15 kg gets 30 J, with subsequent shocks doubling to 4 J/kg. One J/kg is too low for the first shock, 4 J/kg is the dose for shocks after the first, and using an adult fixed dose ignores pediatric weight-based dosing entirely.

pa-pharm-l16.q: An 84-year-old is taking diphenhydramine for allergies, oxybutynin for bladder control, and nortriptyline for neuropathic pain, and now presents with new confusion and urinary retention. What is the underlying issue?
choices: Anticholinergic burden: each drug alone seems tolerable, but stacked together they produce delirium, urinary retention, and fall risk in an older adult
This is unrelated to medications and is simply age-related decline
Each of these drugs is safe in unlimited combination in older adults
This pattern indicates serotonin syndrome
pa-pharm-l16.why: Diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, and nortriptyline are each anticholinergic, and their combined effect in an older adult produces delirium, retention, and falls even though each drug alone might seem minor, which is why the total anticholinergic burden must be considered, not just individual drugs. Serotonin syndrome involves clonus and hyperreflexia, not this picture, and this presentation is drug-driven, not simple aging.

pa-pharm-l16.q: A patient on clopidogrel after a coronary stent is also prescribed omeprazole for reflux. What is the pharmacologic concern?
choices: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, reducing activation of the clopidogrel prodrug and raising the risk of stent thrombosis; pantoprazole is preferred instead
Omeprazole has no interaction with clopidogrel
Clopidogrel will cause omeprazole to lose its acid-suppressing effect
The combination causes serotonin syndrome
pa-pharm-l16.why: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation to become its active form, and omeprazole's strong inhibition of that enzyme can blunt platelet inhibition, raising stent thrombosis risk, which is why pantoprazole (a weaker CYP2C19 inhibitor) is favored. There is a real interaction here, it runs from the PPI toward clopidogrel rather than the reverse, and serotonin syndrome is unrelated to either drug.

pa-pharm-l17.q: A hospitalized patient has a persistent low-grade fever, looks otherwise well, and has no identifiable infectious source despite a full workup. The fever resolves 3 days after a beta-lactam antibiotic is stopped. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Drug fever, a diagnosis of exclusion that classically resolves within about 72 hours of stopping the offending agent
Undiagnosed sepsis that resolved on its own
This must be serotonin syndrome
This confirms a true IgE-mediated antibiotic allergy
pa-pharm-l17.why: Drug fever presents in a well-appearing patient with no clear source and characteristically resolves within about 3 days of stopping the culprit drug, commonly a beta-lactam or anticonvulsant. It is not evidence of self-resolving sepsis, it lacks the neuromuscular findings of serotonin syndrome, and it is a distinct mechanism from classic IgE allergy.

pa-pharm-l17.q: Two to eight weeks after starting allopurinol, a patient develops fever, a widespread rash, facial swelling, and abnormal liver tests with a high eosinophil count. What is this, and what is notable about its course?
choices: DRESS syndrome, which can relapse for weeks even after the drug is stopped
Anaphylaxis, treated with epinephrine
Serotonin syndrome, treated with cyproheptadine
A simple drug rash that resolves within a day of stopping the drug
pa-pharm-l17.why: DRESS presents 2-8 weeks after exposure with fever, rash, facial edema, eosinophilia, and organ involvement (often hepatitis), and unlike a simple rash it can relapse for weeks after the drug is discontinued. It is not anaphylaxis (which is minutes, not weeks, in onset) and it has no relationship to serotonin syndrome.

pa-pharm-l18.q: A patient overdosed on verapamil is hypotensive and bradycardic despite calcium administration. What is the next targeted therapy?
choices: High-dose insulin (1 unit/kg bolus then infusion) with dextrose to support cardiac contractility
Naloxone
N-acetylcysteine
Flumazenil
pa-pharm-l18.why: Calcium channel blocker overdose is treated with calcium first and then hyperinsulinemia-euglycemia therapy, which acts as a powerful inotrope in this setting alongside dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia. Naloxone treats opioids, N-acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen, and flumazenil treats benzodiazepines, none of which address calcium channel blockade.

pa-pharm-l18.q: A child with a topical benzocaine exposure has a pulse oximeter reading stuck near 85% despite a clear airway and chocolate-brown-appearing blood on a sample. What treatment is indicated?
choices: Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV
Deferoxamine
Pyridoxine 5 g IV
Hydroxocobalamin
pa-pharm-l18.why: Benzocaine is a classic cause of methemoglobinemia, which produces a pulse oximeter reading fixed near 85% and chocolate-colored blood; methylene blue restores hemoglobin's oxygen-carrying capacity. Deferoxamine treats iron poisoning, pyridoxine treats isoniazid-induced seizures, and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide, none of which fit this picture.

pa-pharm-l19.q: A patient's potassium remains low despite two rounds of IV potassium replacement, and the magnesium level has not been checked. What is the likely explanation?
choices: A magnesium-depleted kidney continues to waste potassium regardless of how much potassium is given, so magnesium must be replaced alongside it
The potassium dose was simply too small and should be doubled
Potassium replacement never works when given IV
This suggests the patient has factitious hypokalemia
pa-pharm-l19.why: Magnesium is required for the kidney to properly conserve potassium, so a magnesium deficit causes ongoing potassium wasting that will not correct until magnesium is also replaced. Simply increasing the potassium dose ignores the underlying mechanism, IV potassium does work when the deficit is addressed appropriately, and there is no reason from this scenario to suspect factitious illness.

pa-pharm-l19.q: A patient needs IV calcium replaced urgently and a central line is not yet available. Why is calcium gluconate chosen over calcium chloride for peripheral administration?
choices: Calcium chloride contains about three times the elemental calcium per gram and sclerose peripheral veins, so it is reserved for central access, while calcium gluconate is gentler peripherally
Calcium gluconate contains more elemental calcium than calcium chloride
Calcium chloride cannot treat hyperkalemia
There is no difference between the two formulations
pa-pharm-l19.why: Gram for gram, calcium chloride delivers roughly three times the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate and is more caustic to peripheral veins, so it is preferred through a central line while gluconate is used peripherally. Calcium chloride does stabilize the myocardium in hyperkalemia just as gluconate does, just with a stronger effect per gram, and the two formulations are clinically distinct, not interchangeable.

quiz.q: A patient is switched from IV digoxin to oral digoxin at the same total daily amount. Why might the effect change even though the number of milligrams stays the same?
choices: Oral bioavailability is not 100%, so the same milligram number delivers less active drug than the IV dose did
Digoxin cannot be given orally at all
IV and oral digoxin always have identical bioavailability
Digoxin has a large volume of distribution, so a loading strategy matters more than the route itself
quiz.why: Unless the oral dose is adjusted upward to account for incomplete absorption, switching from IV (100% bioavailable) to oral at the identical milligram amount under-delivers active drug. Volume of distribution affects loading dose sizing but does not itself explain the bioavailability gap, digoxin is in fact commonly given orally, and IV and oral bioavailability are not the same for most drugs including digoxin.

quiz.q: Two different oral drugs list bioavailability ranges of 8% and 85%. What does this range primarily reflect?
choices: The manufacturing cost of the drug
How much of each swallowed dose survives absorption and first-pass liver metabolism before reaching the bloodstream
The color and size of the tablet
Whether the drug is a controlled substance
quiz.why: Oral bioavailability varies widely because different drugs are absorbed to different degrees and are destroyed by first-pass hepatic metabolism to different degrees; a drug like morphine sits near the low end while many others are absorbed far more completely. Tablet appearance, controlled-substance status, and manufacturing cost have no bearing on bioavailability.

quiz.q: An elderly patient given atropine for bradycardia becomes acutely confused, while a patient given glycopyrrolate for the same indication does not. What best explains the difference?
choices: Atropine has no effect on the central nervous system
Confusion is unrelated to either drug and is coincidental
Atropine is lipophilic and crosses the blood-brain barrier, while glycopyrrolate is charged and largely does not
Glycopyrrolate is a stronger anticholinergic overall
quiz.why: Atropine's small, lipophilic structure lets it cross into the brain and cause central anticholinergic effects such as confusion, while glycopyrrolate's permanently charged structure keeps it out of the central nervous system, making it the preferred antimuscarinic when central effects are unwanted. Glycopyrrolate is not a stronger anticholinergic overall, and the mechanism is a real, well-described drug effect rather than coincidence.

quiz.q: A patient is known to be a CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizer and is given a standard dose of codeine for pain after surgery. What is the concern?
choices: Ultra-rapid metabolizers get no analgesic effect from codeine at all
This genotype has no clinical relevance for codeine dosing
The concern only applies to children, never adults
Excess conversion of codeine to morphine can produce dangerous, even fatal, opioid toxicity
quiz.why: Because codeine is a prodrug activated to morphine by CYP2D6, an ultra-rapid metabolizer converts an unusually large fraction of the dose, producing higher-than-expected morphine levels and a real risk of respiratory depression; this is why codeine is avoided in known ultra-rapid metabolizers and in breastfeeding mothers of young infants. Poor metabolizers, not ultra-rapid ones, get little effect, and while the historical warning centers on nursing infants, the mechanism applies to any ultra-rapid metabolizer.

quiz.q: A drug has a half-life of 24 hours. Approximately how long does it take to reach steady state on a fixed daily dosing schedule?
choices: 4 to 5 days
10 days
1 day
2 days
quiz.why: Steady state is reached after 4 to 5 half-lives regardless of the dosing interval, so a 24-hour half-life needs about 4 to 5 days to plateau. One or two days represents only 1 to 2 half-lives, which is far short of steady state, and 10 days is roughly 10 half-lives, well beyond what is needed.

quiz.q: A patient stable on simvastatin begins drinking a glass of grapefruit juice with breakfast daily. What is the expected pharmacologic consequence?
choices: Grapefruit only affects drugs given intravenously
Grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, raising simvastatin exposure and the risk of rhabdomyolysis
Grapefruit induces CYP3A4, lowering simvastatin levels and cholesterol control
There is no interaction between grapefruit and statins
quiz.why: Grapefruit blocks CYP3A4 in the gut wall, letting more of an oral CYP3A4-substrate drug like simvastatin survive into the bloodstream, which can multiply exposure and trigger muscle breakdown. It is an inhibitor, not an inducer, the interaction is well established for CYP3A4-metabolized statins, and it specifically affects oral bioavailability, so it is not limited to IV drugs (and statins are given orally in any case).

quiz.q: A patient maintained on methadone for opioid use disorder is given buprenorphine for breakthrough pain management and rapidly develops sweating, cramping, and agitation. What happened?
choices: Methadone and buprenorphine have no receptor interaction
This represents a normal, expected analgesic response
Buprenorphine's strong receptor affinity displaced the full agonist methadone, and its partial agonist ceiling precipitated withdrawal
Buprenorphine caused an allergic reaction
quiz.why: Because buprenorphine binds mu receptors more tightly than methadone but activates them less, substituting it abruptly can knock a full agonist off the receptor and deliver a net drop in stimulation, provoking precipitated withdrawal — a recognized risk when starting buprenorphine in someone on a full agonist. This is a pharmacodynamic interaction, not an allergy, both drugs act at the same mu receptor, and this presentation is withdrawal, not the intended analgesic effect.

quiz.q: Buprenorphine is considered comparatively safer than a full opioid agonist in overdose. What pharmacologic property explains this?
choices: It has no affinity for the mu receptor
It is metabolized to naloxone in the body
It causes no analgesia and therefore no respiratory depression
As a partial agonist it has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression that a full agonist does not have
quiz.why: A partial agonist's effect plateaus below the maximum a full agonist can produce, so buprenorphine's respiratory depression has a ceiling even as the dose increases, unlike morphine or fentanyl. It does bind the mu receptor (strongly, in fact), it is not converted to naloxone, and it does provide real analgesia despite the ceiling.

quiz.q: Which receptor-drug pairing is correctly matched?
choices: Histamine H2 blockade by famotidine reduces stomach acid secretion
Muscarinic blockade by atropine slows the heart rate
Dopamine D2 blockade by haloperidol promotes vomiting
GABA-A activation by benzodiazepines causes wakefulness
quiz.why: H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells drive acid secretion, and famotidine blocking them reduces acid output, exactly the correct pairing. Muscarinic blockade speeds, not slows, the heart; D2 blockade suppresses, not promotes, vomiting (which is why haloperidol and metoclopramide are antiemetics); and GABA-A activation sedates rather than causing wakefulness.

quiz.q: An order calls for 25 g of dextrose for severe hypoglycemia. Using a standard D50 syringe (50% dextrose), what volume delivers this dose?
choices: 25 mL
50 mL
100 mL
quiz.why: D50 is 50 g of dextrose per 100 mL, or 0.5 g/mL, so 25 g requires 50 mL, which is exactly the standard prefilled D50 syringe. The smaller volumes underdose the patient, and 100 mL would deliver double the intended 25 g dose.

quiz.q: A dopamine infusion is mixed as 400 mg in 250 mL and ordered at 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg patient. What is the pump rate?
choices: 40 mL/h
6 mL/h
15 mL/h
24 mL/h
quiz.why: 400 mg in 250 mL is 1,600 mcg/mL. The ordered dose is 5 mcg/kg/min times 80 kg, or 400 mcg/min, which is 24,000 mcg/h. Dividing 24,000 mcg/h by 1,600 mcg/mL gives 15 mL/h; the other values come from errors converting minutes to hours or milligrams to micrograms.

quiz.q: A gravity IV set has a drip factor of 10 gtt/mL and is ordered to run at 125 mL/h. What is the correct drip rate?
choices: About 42 gtt/min
About 125 gtt/min
About 10 gtt/min
About 21 gtt/min
quiz.why: Drops per minute equals mL/h times the drip factor divided by 60, so 125 times 10 divided by 60 is about 20.8, rounding to about 21 gtt/min. Ten gtt/min would under-deliver the fluid substantially, 42 gtt/min roughly doubles the intended rate, and 125 gtt/min ignores the drip factor conversion entirely.

quiz.q: A patient with a documented history of aspirin-induced bronchospasm needs pain control for a sprained ankle. Which agent should be avoided?
choices: Ibuprofen
A lidocaine patch
Oxycodone
Acetaminophen
quiz.why: NSAIDs including ibuprofen share the cyclooxygenase-blocking mechanism that shifts arachidonic acid toward bronchoconstricting leukotrienes, so any NSAID risks triggering bronchospasm in this patient. Acetaminophen has weak, largely central cyclooxygenase activity and is generally tolerated, and topical lidocaine and oxycodone act through entirely different mechanisms unrelated to prostaglandin synthesis.

quiz.q: During a nerve block, a patient develops perioral tingling and a metallic taste in the mouth, then begins to seize seconds later. What is happening and what treatment is indicated?
choices: Malignant hyperthermia, treated with dantrolene
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity; treat with 20% lipid emulsion in addition to seizure and airway management
A normal, expected sensation from the local anesthetic that requires no action
Anaphylaxis, treated with epinephrine 0.3 mg IM as the primary therapy
quiz.why: Perioral tingling and metallic taste are early warning signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity progressing toward seizures and cardiac arrhythmia, and lipid emulsion acts as a lipid sink to pull the drug off cardiac tissue while seizures and the airway are managed. This is not a benign sensation, it is not the IgE-mediated picture of anaphylaxis, and it is unrelated to the anesthetic-trigger mechanism of malignant hyperthermia.

quiz.q: A patient on chronic opioid therapy for cancer pain has developed tolerance to the sedation and nausea but still reports significant constipation despite months of therapy. Why does constipation persist when other side effects fade?
choices: Constipation is unrelated to opioid use and points to a separate diagnosis
Tolerance to constipation develops faster than tolerance to analgesia
Tolerance develops to most mu receptor effects over time, but tolerance to the gut's opioid receptors is minimal, so constipation rarely improves
This indicates the patient has developed an allergy to the opioid
quiz.why: Opioid receptors in the gastrointestinal tract show little to no tolerance compared with the central receptors responsible for sedation, euphoria, and nausea, so constipation typically persists for as long as the opioid is taken and requires ongoing bowel regimen management. This is not an allergy, it is a direct and expected pharmacologic effect, and tolerance to constipation is notably slower to develop, not faster, than tolerance to analgesia.

quiz.q: A hypotensive trauma patient needs rapid sequence intubation. Which induction agent best preserves hemodynamics?
choices: Propofol, because it is the fastest acting agent
Only succinylcholine, since it has no hemodynamic effects itself
Midazolam alone at a high dose
Etomidate or ketamine, both of which have minimal effect on blood pressure
quiz.why: Etomidate barely touches blood pressure and ketamine actually supports it through catecholamine release, making both preferred induction choices in a hemodynamically unstable patient, whereas propofol drops blood pressure hard and is generally avoided here. Succinylcholine is a paralytic, not an induction agent, and does not itself address sedation or hemodynamics, and high-dose midazolam alone is not a standard RSI induction approach and still risks hypotension.

quiz.q: Fosphenytoin is being loaded for status epilepticus and the pharmacist warns against pushing it too quickly. What happens if the infusion runs faster than the recommended rate?
choices: Hypotension and arrhythmia, and tissue injury if it infiltrates the vein
Immediate seizure cessation with no other effect
It has no rate-related toxicity, unlike phenytoin
It causes rapid-onset serotonin syndrome
quiz.why: Phenytoin (and, to a lesser extent, its prodrug fosphenytoin) must be infused slowly, no faster than about 50 mg/min for phenytoin, because rapid infusion causes hypotension, arrhythmia, and tissue damage on extravasation. It does not instantly stop seizures with no other risk, the rate-related toxicity is a real concern for fosphenytoin as well (though reduced compared with phenytoin), and it has no relationship to serotonin syndrome.

quiz.q: A patient paralyzed with rocuronium for a procedure needs rapid reversal because the airway could not be secured. What is the appropriate reversal agent?
choices: Physostigmine
Sugammadex 16 mg/kg
Naloxone
Flumazenil
quiz.why: Sugammadex directly encapsulates rocuronium (and vecuronium), rapidly reversing paralysis even from a deep block, which is exactly why rocuronium became a viable alternative to succinylcholine despite its longer duration. Naloxone reverses opioids, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity, none of which reverse neuromuscular blockade.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old on chronic prednisone is started on ciprofloxacin for a urinary infection and three days later develops sudden heel pain while walking. What should be suspected?
choices: An allergic reaction to ciprofloxacin
Normal muscle soreness from increased activity
Fluoroquinolone-associated Achilles tendinopathy or rupture, a risk amplified by concurrent corticosteroid use and older age
A simple ankle sprain unrelated to medication
quiz.why: Fluoroquinolones are linked to tendinopathy and rupture, most classically at the Achilles tendon, and the risk rises sharply with age and concurrent corticosteroid therapy, both present here. This is a specific, recognized drug toxicity rather than a coincidental sprain or soreness, and it is a direct tissue effect rather than an IgE-mediated allergy.

quiz.q: A critically ill patient with suspected hospital-acquired pneumonia and possible Pseudomonas needs broad empiric coverage that also includes anaerobes. Which agent fits best?
choices: Amoxicillin
Doxycycline
Nitrofurantoin
Piperacillin-tazobactam
quiz.why: Piperacillin-tazobactam is the broad-spectrum IV penicillin that covers Pseudomonas and anaerobes together, making it a workhorse choice for severe hospital-acquired infections. Amoxicillin and doxycycline lack Pseudomonas coverage, and nitrofurantoin is limited to uncomplicated cystitis and does not achieve therapeutic lung tissue levels.

quiz.q: A pregnant patient with a tick bite and early signs of Lyme disease is a candidate for doxycycline. What should guide this decision?
choices: Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy for Lyme disease because amoxicillin and cefuroxime axetil are proven alternatives; the 2020 IDSA guideline treats pregnant patients exactly like non-pregnant ones except that doxycycline is omitted
Tetracyclines are absolutely avoided at any point in pregnancy under all circumstances with no exceptions considered
Doxycycline has no known effects on pregnancy or fetal development
Only intravenous vancomycin can be used for Lyme disease in pregnancy
quiz.why: The 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR Lyme guideline states that pregnant and lactating patients are treated the same as everyone else except that doxycycline is avoided, because amoxicillin and cefuroxime axetil are proven alternatives and tetracyclines can stain developing teeth and affect bone growth. The avoidance is not absolute across every tetracycline indication (short-course doxycycline is accepted for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, where no equivalent alternative exists), doxycycline does have recognized fetal effects, and vancomycin is not a Lyme treatment.

quiz.q: A patient with a creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min needs venous thromboembolism treatment. What is the correct approach to enoxaparin dosing?
choices: Avoid checking renal function since enoxaparin requires no monitoring regardless
Reduce the dose because enoxaparin accumulates in significant renal impairment
Give the standard 1 mg/kg dose with no change
Double the dose to ensure adequate anticoagulation
quiz.why: Enoxaparin is renally cleared, and significant impairment (commonly a threshold near creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min) requires a reduced dose to avoid drug accumulation and bleeding, even though routine monitoring is otherwise unnecessary in normal renal function. The standard unadjusted dose risks overdosing this patient, doubling it would be dangerous, and while routine anti-Xa monitoring is not typical, renal function still must guide the dose.

quiz.q: A patient receiving a drug-eluting coronary stent is placed on clopidogrel but is later found to be a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. What is the clinical concern?
choices: CYP2C19 status has no effect on clopidogrel
This genotype only matters for warfarin, not clopidogrel
Inadequate activation of the clopidogrel prodrug can leave the patient under-protected against stent thrombosis
Poor metabolizers get excess drug effect and bleed more
quiz.why: Clopidogrel requires CYP2C19 activation to become pharmacologically active, so a poor metabolizer converts less of the prodrug, achieves less platelet inhibition, and faces a real risk of stent thrombosis, which is why some patients are switched to prasugrel or ticagrelor, which do not depend as heavily on this pathway. The effect is reduced, not increased, activity, CYP2C19 genotype is highly relevant to clopidogrel specifically, and warfarin's metabolism involves a different enzyme (CYP2C9) entirely.

quiz.q: A patient presenting with an acute ischemic stroke within the treatment window has a blood pressure of 192/114 that has not yet been treated. What is the status of thrombolysis?
choices: It is an absolute, permanent contraindication regardless of treatment
Blood pressure has no bearing on thrombolysis eligibility
Thrombolysis should be given immediately regardless of pressure to save time
It is held until blood pressure is brought below 185/110, since uncontrolled severe hypertension is a contraindication that can often be corrected
quiz.why: A pressure above 185/110 is a contraindication to thrombolysis, but unlike a prior intracranial hemorrhage, it is often correctable with antihypertensive treatment, after which thrombolysis can proceed within the window if otherwise eligible. It is not a permanent disqualifier, blood pressure very much matters for bleeding risk during thrombolysis, and giving the drug before addressing severe hypertension raises the risk of intracranial hemorrhage.

quiz.q: A patient with reactive airway disease needs beta blockade for rate control but the team is uncertain how they will tolerate it. Which agent allows the fastest ability to stop the effect if bronchospasm worsens?
choices: Esmolol, due to its roughly 9-minute duration of action
Atenolol, given once daily
Propranolol, due to its long half-life
Carvedilol, due to its combined alpha and beta blockade
quiz.why: Esmolol's very short duration lets clinicians essentially test the effect of beta blockade and let it dissipate quickly if bronchospasm develops, which is valuable in a patient with reactive airway disease. Atenolol and propranolol have much longer durations that would persist if trouble developed, and carvedilol's added alpha blockade does not shorten its duration.

quiz.q: A patient on digoxin for atrial fibrillation develops nausea, confusion, and reports seeing yellow-green halos around lights. A recent diuretic dose caused a low potassium. What is the connection?
choices: Digoxin toxicity only causes cardiac symptoms, never visual disturbances
Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding to its target, worsening toxicity even without a dose change
Potassium level has no bearing on digoxin toxicity
This is an unrelated visual migraine
quiz.why: Low potassium enhances digoxin's binding to the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, worsening toxicity at the same drug level, which is why potassium is corrected in any patient with suspected digoxin toxicity. Visual disturbances, specifically yellow-green halos, are a classic and well-described feature of digoxin toxicity, not a separate migraine process, and potassium is directly relevant to its toxicity.

quiz.q: A patient in cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation has received defibrillation, epinephrine, and amiodarone 300 mg without return of circulation. What is an appropriate next antiarrhythmic option if amiodarone is unavailable for the second dose?
choices: Digoxin immune Fab
Flumazenil
Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV
Adenosine 6 mg IV push
quiz.why: Lidocaine is the recognized alternative antiarrhythmic to amiodarone in shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Adenosine is for stable narrow-complex SVT, not arrest rhythms, digoxin immune Fab treats digoxin toxicity, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, none of which are arrest antiarrhythmics.

quiz.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes and stable chronic kidney disease is scheduled for a CT with IV contrast. What is the correct approach to metformin?
choices: Continue metformin with no changes since it has no interaction with contrast
Stop metformin permanently and switch to insulin for life
Double the metformin dose before the scan to compensate for contrast effects
Hold metformin around the time of contrast administration due to the risk of contrast-associated kidney injury precipitating lactic acidosis
quiz.why: Metformin is temporarily held around contrast exposure because acute kidney injury from contrast can let the drug accumulate and trigger lactic acidosis; it is typically restarted once renal function is confirmed stable, not stopped forever. Continuing without any consideration ignores a real, described risk, and doubling the dose before the scan would be actively dangerous.

quiz.q: An elderly patient found unresponsive with a glucose of 38 mg/dL is discovered to take glipizide. After IV dextrose raises the glucose to normal, what is the appropriate disposition?
choices: Admission for observation, since sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia can recur for many hours as insulin secretion continues
Immediate discharge once the glucose normalizes, since the danger has passed
No further glucose monitoring is needed after one normal reading
Discharge with instructions to eat more food at home
quiz.why: Because sulfonylureas keep stimulating insulin release long after a single dextrose correction, hypoglycemia can recur for hours, so these patients require admission and monitoring rather than a one-time treatment and discharge. A single normal glucose does not mean the risk has passed, and discharge instructions alone do not address ongoing insulin secretion.

quiz.q: Albuterol is sometimes used as an adjunct treatment for hyperkalemia. What is the mechanism?
choices: Albuterol has no established role in hyperkalemia management
Beta-2 stimulation drives potassium into cells, temporarily lowering serum levels
Albuterol binds and removes potassium from the body
Albuterol works by causing diuresis of potassium through the kidney
quiz.why: Beta-2 agonism activates the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, shifting potassium intracellularly and temporarily lowering the serum level, the same shift mechanism used by insulin, which is why nebulized albuterol is a recognized adjunct in hyperkalemia treatment. It does not remove potassium from the body (only shifting agents do that; removal requires binders, dialysis, or diuresis), and it does not work through renal excretion.

quiz.q: A patient with a rapidly spreading leg infection has pain far exceeding what the skin findings suggest, along with skin discoloration and a low-grade fever. Imaging shows gas in the soft tissue. What is the priority?
choices: Bedside incision and drainage only
Observation with serial exams over 24 hours before deciding on treatment
Emergency surgical consultation for debridement, plus broad antibiotics including clindamycin, rather than antibiotics alone
Oral antibiotics with outpatient follow-up in 48 hours
quiz.why: Gas in the soft tissue with pain out of proportion to exam findings strongly suggests necrotizing fasciitis, which requires emergent surgical debridement as the definitive treatment; antibiotics support but cannot substitute for source control. Oral therapy, simple drainage, or watchful observation all risk fatal delay in a condition that can progress within hours.

quiz.q: A sexually active woman presents with lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, and fever, consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease. Which regimen matches current treatment recommendations?
choices: A single dose of oral fluconazole
Nitrofurantoin for 5 days
Vancomycin alone
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM, plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
quiz.why: PID treatment must cover gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes together, which is exactly what ceftriaxone plus doxycycline plus metronidazole for 14 days accomplishes. Fluconazole treats fungal infections, nitrofurantoin treats cystitis, and vancomycin alone leaves gonorrhea and chlamydia untreated.

quiz.q: A patient with an intra-abdominal abscess undergoes percutaneous drainage and is started on antibiotics. How long should antibiotics generally continue once source control is achieved?
choices: About 4 days after adequate source control, not a fixed long course regardless of drainage
A minimum of 14 days no matter what
Antibiotics can be stopped immediately after drainage with no further course
Antibiotics should continue indefinitely until symptoms fully resolve, however long that takes
quiz.why: Once the source is adequately controlled, evidence supports a short course, commonly around 4 days, rather than an arbitrarily long fixed duration; source control, not prolonged antibiotics, does the real work. Stopping entirely at the moment of drainage ignores residual bacterial burden, and open-ended indefinite courses promote resistance without added benefit once the source is controlled.

quiz.q: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and no history of diabetes is being optimized on guideline-directed therapy. Should an SGLT2 inhibitor be added?
choices: Only if the patient already failed three other heart failure medications
Yes, SGLT2 inhibitors lower mortality in HFrEF independent of diabetes status
No, SGLT2 inhibitors only benefit patients with diabetes
No, SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated in heart failure
quiz.why: SGLT2 inhibitors are one of the four pillar therapies for HFrEF and reduce mortality and hospitalization regardless of whether the patient has diabetes, so diabetes status should not gate their use. They are not contraindicated in heart failure (quite the opposite), and they are added alongside, not only after failing, other pillar therapies.

quiz.q: A patient in narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 180 beats per minute is hypotensive with altered mental status. What is the correct next step?
choices: Oral metoprolol
Observation, since narrow-complex tachycardias are rarely dangerous
Synchronized cardioversion, because the instability, not the rhythm classification, dictates immediate electricity over drugs
Adenosine 6 mg IV push first, since it is first line for any narrow regular tachycardia
quiz.why: Instability (hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic pain, or acute heart failure caused by the rhythm) means electrical treatment takes priority over pharmacologic options regardless of whether the rhythm is narrow or wide. Adenosine is appropriate for a stable narrow regular tachycardia, not an unstable one, oral medication is far too slow for this presentation, and observation ignores clear instability.

quiz.q: A patient with confirmed triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome and a history of clots is being considered for anticoagulation. Which agent is preferred?
choices: Apixaban, because DOACs are preferred in almost every situation
No anticoagulation is required in antiphospholipid syndrome
Aspirin alone is sufficient regardless of clot history
Warfarin, because DOACs have shown inferior outcomes in this specific population
quiz.why: Triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome is one of the specific situations where DOACs underperform compared with warfarin, joining mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis as an exception to the usual DOAC preference. Given the strong thrombotic tendency, anticoagulation is indicated, not withheld, and aspirin alone is inadequate for someone with an established clot history from this condition.

quiz.q: A postoperative order set has acetaminophen and ibuprofen written as PRN (as needed) rather than scheduled. What is the likely consequence compared with scheduled dosing?
choices: Total drug use, including opioid use, tends to be higher because pain that has already peaked is harder to control
PRN dosing always uses less total medication than scheduled dosing
There is no meaningful difference between PRN and scheduled non-opioid dosing
PRN dosing eliminates the need for opioids entirely
quiz.why: Waiting for pain to become bad enough to request medication (PRN) lets pain escalate before treatment starts, generally requiring more total drug, including more opioid, to regain control compared with staying ahead of pain with scheduled multimodal dosing. It is not the case that PRN uses less total medication, some difference clearly exists between the strategies, and neither approach eliminates opioid need in significant pain by itself.

quiz.q: A patient with multiple rib fractures is breathing shallowly due to pain and is at risk for pneumonia. Which intervention specifically helps by allowing deeper breathing without heavy systemic opioid sedation?
choices: A fentanyl patch
A serratus anterior regional block
IV morphine alone at escalating doses
Oral acetaminophen alone
quiz.why: A serratus anterior block provides targeted regional analgesia to the chest wall, allowing deeper breathing and coughing that helps prevent pneumonia, without the systemic sedation that escalating IV opioids bring. Opioid escalation alone risks respiratory depression that worsens shallow breathing, acetaminophen alone is unlikely to control rib fracture pain sufficiently, and a fentanyl patch is both too slow to start and inappropriate for acute, changing pain.

quiz.q: A patient is converted from home oral oxycodone to IV hydromorphone using the full calculated equianalgesic dose with no reduction, and becomes oversedated. What principle was violated?
choices: Hydromorphone cannot be given by the IV route
The patient must have developed a new drug allergy
Incomplete cross-tolerance between different opioids means a calculated equianalgesic dose should be reduced by about 25-50%
Equianalgesic conversion tables are inaccurate and should never be used
quiz.why: Tolerance to one mu agonist does not transfer completely to a different opioid, so using the full calculated equianalgesic dose during a switch risks overdose; reducing the calculated dose by 25-50% accounts for this incomplete cross-tolerance. The conversion tables themselves are a legitimate starting point, IV hydromorphone is a standard and common route, and oversedation from a dosing error is not evidence of a new allergy.

quiz.q: A patient abruptly stops taking venlafaxine after several months and within a day develops dizziness, nausea, and brief electric-shock-like sensations. What is the best management?
choices: Start flumazenil immediately
Diagnose serotonin syndrome and give cyproheptadine
Reassure the patient that no medication-related cause is possible
Restart the medication and taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly in the future
quiz.why: This is antidepressant discontinuation syndrome, most notable with short-half-life agents like venlafaxine and paroxetine, and management is to restart and taper slowly rather than stop abruptly again. Flumazenil has no role here (it reverses benzodiazepines), this is not serotonin syndrome (there is no excess serotonergic drug on board causing hyperactivation), and the presentation is a well-recognized medication effect, not something to dismiss.

quiz.q: A patient wants to switch from fluoxetine to an MAO inhibitor for treatment-resistant depression. What washout period is required and why?
choices: About 5 weeks after fluoxetine, because its long-acting metabolite persists and combining it with an MAOI risks a severe serotonergic and hypertensive crisis
No washout is needed since both classes raise serotonin similarly
A 24-hour washout is sufficient for any antidepressant switch
MAOIs and SSRIs are safe to combine as long as doses are low
quiz.why: Fluoxetine's active metabolite has an unusually long half-life, so a roughly 5-week washout (compared with about 2 weeks for most other antidepressants) is required before starting an MAOI to avoid a dangerous interaction combining serotonin syndrome risk with the MAOI's own tyramine-related hypertensive crisis potential. Both classes raising serotonin is exactly why they cannot be combined safely, a short 24-hour gap is far too brief, and there is no safe low-dose combination of these classes.

quiz.q: A patient on clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia reports new chest discomfort, fatigue, and shortness of breath weeks after starting the drug. Beyond agranulocytosis, what serious complication should be considered?
choices: This is always simple anxiety related to starting a new medication
Myocarditis, which clozapine can cause and which requires prompt cardiac evaluation
This is expected and requires no further workup
Clozapine has no cardiac risks of any kind
quiz.why: Clozapine carries a recognized risk of myocarditis in addition to agranulocytosis and seizures, and new cardiopulmonary symptoms in a patient on clozapine warrant prompt cardiac workup rather than assumption of anxiety. It is not an expected, benign finding, clozapine does carry real cardiac risk, and dismissing the symptoms as purely psychological could miss a serious complication.

quiz.q: Using the standard formula, what cuffed endotracheal tube size is appropriate for a 12-year-old?
quiz.why: The cuffed tube formula is age divided by 4 plus 3.5, so 12 divided by 4 is 3, plus 3.5 gives 6.5. The other values reflect skipping the division, using the uncuffed constant instead, or an incorrect calculation.

quiz.q: A 20 kg child is in pulseless ventricular fibrillation and has already received one 40 J shock without return of circulation. What is the correct energy for the second shock?
choices: 40 J, the same as before
20 J (1 J/kg)
100 J, the standard adult dose
80 J (4 J/kg)
quiz.why: After the initial 2 J/kg shock, subsequent pediatric defibrillation doses double to 4 J/kg, so 20 kg receives 80 J on the second shock. Repeating the same energy or using a lower energy does not follow the escalation protocol, and a fixed adult dose ignores pediatric weight-based dosing.

quiz.q: A 16 kg child is prescribed amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for acute otitis media. What is the correct dose per administration?
choices: 720 mg per dose
1,440 mg per dose
90 mg per dose
360 mg per dose
quiz.why: 90 mg/kg times 16 kg is 1,440 mg per day, and dividing that by two doses gives 720 mg per dose. 1,440 mg would be the full daily total given as if it were a single dose, 90 mg ignores the weight multiplication entirely, and 360 mg would result from dividing by four doses instead of two.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old on diphenhydramine for sleep, oxybutynin for overactive bladder, and amitriptyline for neuropathic pain develops new confusion, dry mouth, and urinary retention. What is the best explanation and management?
choices: Increasing all three doses will resolve the confusion
Cumulative anticholinergic burden from three separate drugs; deprescribing the least necessary agents is the priority
A single new drug allergy that requires switching to a chemically unrelated class of just one drug
This is unrelated to medications and requires only a urinary catheter
quiz.why: Each of these three drugs carries anticholinergic activity, and their combined burden in an older adult produces delirium, dry mouth, and retention even though any single drug might seem tolerable alone, so the management is to reduce or eliminate unnecessary anticholinergic agents. This is not a single-drug allergy, ignoring the medication list and treating only the retention misses the cause, and increasing the doses would worsen the picture.

quiz.q: A patient is prescribed an opioid for pain, already takes a benzodiazepine for anxiety and gabapentin for neuropathy, and also drinks alcohol regularly. What is the primary concern with this combination?
choices: Only the opioid and alcohol combination matters; the others are irrelevant
This combination only becomes dangerous if all four are taken at exactly the same minute
Additive central nervous system and respiratory depression from stacking multiple sedating drugs, a common pattern in fatal overdoses
None of these drugs interact with each other at all
quiz.why: Opioids, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, and alcohol each independently depress the central nervous system and breathing, and stacking several of them, each individually prescribed or legal, is a recognized and common contributor to fatal respiratory depression. There is a real, additive interaction among all of them, not just the opioid-alcohol pair, and the danger builds from the combined drug burden over the dosing period, not only from simultaneous timing.

quiz.q: A patient on clopidogrel after stent placement is started on a proton pump inhibitor for reflux symptoms. Which PPI choice minimizes the interaction risk with clopidogrel's activation?
choices: Omeprazole, because it has the strongest acid suppression
Any PPI is equally safe since none interact with clopidogrel
The class should be avoided entirely regardless of clinical need
Pantoprazole, because it is a weaker CYP2C19 inhibitor than omeprazole
quiz.why: Because clopidogrel requires CYP2C19 activation, and omeprazole inhibits that enzyme more strongly than pantoprazole, pantoprazole is generally preferred in patients who need both a PPI and clopidogrel. Omeprazole's stronger acid suppression does not offset its stronger CYP2C19 interaction, PPIs are not interchangeable here, and reflux still often needs treatment, so blanket avoidance ignores that clinical need.

quiz.q: A hospitalized patient looks well, has intermittent fevers, and an extensive infectious workup is negative. The fever resolves within 3 days of stopping a beta-lactam antibiotic. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Drug fever
Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Anaphylaxis
quiz.why: Drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion in a well-appearing patient with no infectious source, and it characteristically resolves within about 3 days of discontinuing the offending drug, commonly a beta-lactam. Serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome present with neuromuscular findings this patient lacks, and anaphylaxis is an acute, minutes-scale reaction, not an intermittent fever pattern over days.

quiz.q: A patient started on allopurinol six weeks ago now has fever, facial swelling, a diffuse rash, and lab tests showing eosinophilia and elevated liver enzymes. What is the expected clinical course?
choices: This always requires epinephrine as first-line treatment
Symptoms may persist or relapse for weeks even after allopurinol is discontinued
Symptoms will resolve completely within hours of stopping the drug
This picture has no relationship to medication and needs no drug review
quiz.why: DRESS syndrome, exactly this presentation, characteristically has a delayed onset (2-8 weeks) and a course that can drag on or relapse for weeks after the culprit drug is stopped, unlike a simple drug rash. It does not resolve within hours, a thorough medication review is essential to identify the cause, and epinephrine is reserved for anaphylaxis, not DRESS.

quiz.q: A patient on methimazole for hyperthyroidism develops a sore throat and fever. What specific laboratory test is the priority?
choices: A rapid strep swab only, with no blood work needed
A liver panel, since methimazole primarily affects the liver
An absolute neutrophil count to evaluate for drug-induced agranulocytosis
A thyroid-stimulating hormone level
quiz.why: Methimazole is one of the drugs, alongside clozapine and ticlopidine, associated with agranulocytosis, so a sore throat and fever in a patient on this drug demands an urgent neutrophil count rather than assuming a routine viral or strep infection. A thyroid level does not address the acute infection risk, skipping blood work risks missing a life-threatening neutropenia, and while methimazole can affect the liver, that is not the most urgent concern for this presentation.

quiz.q: A patient who overdosed on verapamil remains hypotensive and bradycardic after calcium gluconate and atropine. What is the next targeted intervention?
choices: Naloxone 2 mg IV
Physostigmine 2 mg IV
N-acetylcysteine load
High-dose insulin with dextrose to support cardiac contractility
quiz.why: After initial calcium administration, hyperinsulinemia-euglycemia therapy is the next specific treatment for calcium channel blocker toxicity, acting as a potent inotrope while dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. Naloxone treats opioids, physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity (and can be dangerous with cardiotoxic overdoses), and N-acetylcysteine is specific to acetaminophen.

quiz.q: A patient with an accidental large ingestion of iron tablets presents with abdominal pain and vomiting. Which antidote should be prepared?
choices: Deferoxamine
Methylene blue
Pyridoxine
Fomepizole
quiz.why: Deferoxamine chelates iron, forming a complex that can be excreted, and is the specific antidote for significant iron poisoning. Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, pyridoxine treats isoniazid-induced seizures, and fomepizole treats toxic alcohol ingestions such as methanol or ethylene glycol, none of which apply to iron.

quiz.q: A patient who took a large isoniazid overdose develops refractory seizures that do not respond to benzodiazepines. What should be given?
choices: Dantrolene
Pyridoxine 5 g IV
Flumazenil
Hydroxocobalamin
quiz.why: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine (vitamin B6), which is required for GABA synthesis, so isoniazid-induced seizures are specifically treated with high-dose pyridoxine when benzodiazepines alone fail. Flumazenil is unrelated and can worsen seizures in some contexts, hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide, and dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

quiz.q: A patient's serum potassium remains low despite two doses of IV potassium, and the magnesium has not been checked. What is the most likely explanation for the refractory hypokalemia?
choices: This response indicates the patient does not actually have hypokalemia
Refractory hypokalemia after IV replacement is expected and requires no further evaluation
Concurrent hypomagnesemia is causing ongoing renal potassium wasting that will not correct until magnesium is replaced
The IV potassium doses were administered too slowly
quiz.why: A magnesium deficit impairs the kidney's ability to conserve potassium, so potassium replacement alone will not correct the level until magnesium is also repleted, which is why magnesium is checked and treated alongside potassium in refractory cases. Infusion speed is not the issue described, the lab values do reflect real hypokalemia, and this pattern specifically warrants further evaluation (checking magnesium), not simple acceptance.

quiz.q: A patient needs IV calcium replaced urgently and only peripheral IV access is available. Which formulation is preferred and why?
choices: Calcium chloride, because it contains less elemental calcium per gram
Either formulation is identical for peripheral use
Calcium chloride, because it cannot be given through a central line
Calcium gluconate, because calcium chloride is more caustic to peripheral veins and is preferentially reserved for central access
quiz.why: Calcium gluconate is gentler on peripheral veins, while calcium chloride, which actually contains about three times more elemental calcium per gram, is more likely to cause tissue injury peripherally and is preferred through a central line. The two formulations are not interchangeable, and calcium chloride can in fact be given centrally, which is the setting where it is favored.

quiz.q: A chronically hypertensive patient in septic shock is not making adequate urine output despite a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg on norepinephrine. What should be considered?
choices: A higher MAP target, since chronic hypertensives may need 80-85 mmHg to maintain adequate organ perfusion
Stopping norepinephrine immediately since 65 mmHg should always be sufficient
Switching to a pure beta agonist instead of norepinephrine
Concluding that urine output is irrelevant to pressor titration
quiz.why: While 65 mmHg is the typical target mean arterial pressure in shock, chronically hypertensive patients may have a shifted autoregulatory curve and require a higher target, such as 80-85 mmHg, to adequately perfuse the kidneys and other organs, accepting the tradeoff of more arrhythmia risk. Stopping the pressor ignores the patient's poor perfusion, a pure beta agonist does not address the vasodilation of septic shock the way norepinephrine does, and urine output is a key perfusion marker that should inform titration.

quiz.q: A drug that is highly protein bound and confined mostly to the bloodstream is compared with one that distributes widely into fat and muscle. Which statement correctly links volume of distribution to clinical behavior?
choices: Volume of distribution only matters for drugs given orally
The widely distributed drug generally needs a larger loading dose to achieve the same blood concentration as the confined drug
Protein binding has no relationship to volume of distribution
The confined drug always requires a loading dose while the widely distributed one never does
quiz.why: A drug that spreads extensively into tissue has a large apparent volume of distribution and needs proportionally more total drug (often via a loading dose) to reach a given blood concentration compared with a drug that stays mostly in the vascular space. Protein binding does influence the free fraction available to leave the bloodstream and is related to distribution behavior, loading dose need depends on urgency and half-life as much as which drug is confined versus widely distributed, and volume of distribution is a property relevant to any route, not only oral.

quiz.q: A patient on a norepinephrine infusion for septic shock develops extravasation at the peripheral IV site with blanching and pain around it. What is the appropriate treatment for the site?
choices: Discontinuing all vasopressor support immediately
Massaging the area vigorously to redistribute the drug
Local infiltration of phentolamine around the extravasation site
Application of ice only, with no medication
quiz.why: Norepinephrine extravasation causes local vasoconstriction that can lead to tissue necrosis, and phentolamine, an alpha-blocker, is infiltrated locally to reverse that vasoconstriction and preserve the tissue. Ice alone does not reverse the alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction, stopping the pressor entirely is dangerous for a patient in shock and does not address the local injury, and massaging the site can worsen tissue damage.

quiz.q: A patient on an SSRI, a triptan for migraines, and tramadol for pain develops agitation, sweating, and sustained clonus in the ankles within hours of starting the tramadol. Which combination of drugs on this list is most responsible?
choices: The triptan alone, unrelated to the other two drugs
None of these drugs affect serotonin
This is an expected, harmless effect of combining any three medications
The SSRI and tramadol together, both of which raise serotonin, with the triptan adding further risk
quiz.why: SSRIs and tramadol both increase serotonergic activity, and adding a triptan, which also affects serotonin receptors, compounds the risk, producing the classic serotonin syndrome picture of agitation, sweating, and clonus that is worst in the legs. The triptan is not the sole cause in isolation, all three drugs here do affect serotonin, and this is a dangerous, recognized interaction rather than a harmless combination.
